title: Marketing Research Digest — Advertising — 2026-10-09
journals_not_indexed: Journal of Consumer Satisfaction, Dissatisfaction and Complaining Behavior
Journal of Empirical Generalisations in Marketing Science
Marketing Science Institute Working Paper Series

studies.title: When shoppers spot an AI-made ad, they like it less — but still buy
studies.paper_title: Disclosing AI-generated advertising: effects on attitudes, purchase intent, and social media engagement
studies.the_study: Researchers tested "synthetic" out-of-home advertising — AI-altered images of billboards and street installations that brands post on social media as if they were real. They found that the more creative an ad looked, the more persuasive it was, but also the more likely viewers were to realize it wasn't real. Consumers who caught on reported lower attitudes toward both the ad and the brand, yet purchase intent and willingness to engage on social media were unaffected; high creativity softened the attitude penalty.
studies.why_it_matters: Fake-but-spectacular stunt ads have become a staple of brand social feeds, and this suggests the reputational cost of being found out is real but narrow — it dents sentiment without visibly denting commercial intent.
studies.story_angle_primary: Worth testing whether your own synthetic stunt creative crosses the believability line: the study suggests creativity is a double-edged lever that raises both persuasion and detection, so brands could pilot disclosure versus non-disclosure and track brand attitude separately from conversion rather than assuming one proxies for the other.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A reminder for anyone scrolling past a jaw-dropping billboard: many of the most shareable outdoor ads never existed. Noticing the trick makes people think less of the brand — but apparently not enough to change what they buy.
studies.caveats: Experimental study of a single ad format (out-of-home) in a social media context; attitudes and purchase intent are self-reported rather than observed purchases; sample and country details are not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Core findings match, but the headline converts unchanged purchase intent into actual buying and the direction of the creativity moderation is not specified in the abstract.

studies.title: Slashing the ad budget makes your stock look riskier, 231,000 firm-years suggest
studies.paper_title: Massive Advertising Expenses Changes, Risk, and Implications for Stock Returns
studies.the_study: An analysis of 231,323 US firm-year observations examined not the level of advertising spending but the logarithmic percentage change in it, isolating only dramatic swings. Firms that made massive cuts to advertising expenses subsequently showed higher stock returns — the signature of investors pricing in higher risk — an effect described as both economically and statistically significant and holding across multiple robustness tests.
studies.why_it_matters: It puts a capital-markets price tag on the familiar recession reflex of gutting the ad budget: abrupt cuts appear to raise a firm's perceived risk and therefore its cost of equity.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are arguing against a sudden marketing cut, this gives a finance-department argument rather than a marketing one: the paper's implication is that budgets should be adjusted gradually, because the market reads a cliff-edge drop as a risk signal. Worth stress-testing with your own CFO on how your investors have historically reacted to spend changes.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For investors and observers, a brand that suddenly goes quiet in advertising may be telling the market something — and the market appears to notice, demanding higher returns to hold the stock.
studies.caveats: Observational archival data, so associations rather than clean causal identification; US-listed firms only; accounting-reported advertising expense is a crude measure that omits much modern marketing spend.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample size, variable construction and finding match the abstract; archival/correlational limits are flagged in Caveats.

studies.title: Let the AI do the guilt-tripping and keep the humans for the pep talk
studies.paper_title: AI for guilt, human for encouragement? The interaction effects of creator type and emotional appeal on green purchase intention
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Three studies — two scenario-based experiments (one Chinese sample, one international English-speaking online sample) and a field experiment using actual purchase data from a live-streaming retailer — crossed the disclosed creator of a green ad (AI-generated versus human-generated) with its emotional appeal (guilt versus encouragement). AI-generated guilt appeals beat human-generated ones at driving green purchase intention, apparently because an AI scold triggers less "green moral pressure." Human-generated encouragement beat AI-generated encouragement, working through greater green self-efficacy.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes the AI-versus-human creative debate as a matching problem: the same disclosure that hurts one kind of message can help another, with the negative appeals being exactly where machine authorship pays.
studies.story_angle_primary: A concrete A/B test for sustainability and cause marketing: pair guilt or responsibility framings with disclosed AI authorship, and keep human signatures on uplifting, you-can-do-this messaging. The field-experiment leg makes this stronger than most AI-disclosure research, but it is one retailer in one format.
studies.story_angle_secondary: People bristle at being made to feel guilty by another person — but take the same reproach from a machine with less resentment. It is a small window into why moral pressure lands differently depending on who is applying it.
studies.caveats: Two of three studies are scenario-based with stated intentions; the field component comes from a single live-streaming retailer and category; effects may be culture-specific despite the international sample.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, samples and both mediated effects are reported correctly, but the abstract's attribution-focus moderator is dropped.

studies.title: Abstract nature imagery outperforms actual forests in service ads
studies.paper_title: Nature sells: How visual biophilia influences promotional effectiveness of service firms
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Two experiments compared service advertising using direct biophilia (literal images of nature), indirect biophilia (abstract natural patterns, nature-like materials, earthy color schemes) and a no-nature control. Indirect, abstract nature cues produced the most favorable ad evaluations and behavioral intentions, working through perceived novelty and mystery rather than the restorative calm usually attributed to nature imagery. Benefits were largest when the advertised service was conceptually aligned with nature.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the standard stock-photo waterfall may be the weaker option, and that suggestive texture and palette can do more persuasive work than literal greenery.
studies.story_angle_primary: A cheap creative test for service brands — hotels, spas, wellness, financial or health services — swapping literal nature photography for abstracted natural forms and palettes, and measuring novelty and curiosity as the mechanism. Treat it as a hypothesis to validate in-market, not an established rule.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Our pull toward nature in advertising seems to be driven less by relaxation than by intrigue: a hint of the natural world grabs attention more than the full picture does.
studies.caveats: Two experiments only, with ad evaluations and behavioral intentions rather than real bookings or purchases; sample size, sample source and country are not specified in the abstract; limited to service categories.
studies.verdict_notes: Two studies, the indirect-over-direct biophilia result, the novelty/mystery mechanism and the service–nature alignment condition all match the abstract.

studies.title: Kids recorded their own screens for four days — and found an ad every 2.6 minutes of gaming
studies.paper_title: Bombarded? Child’s-eye views of smartphone-based game application advertising: objective insights from Aotearoa New Zealand
studies.the_study: Researchers in Wellington, New Zealand recruited 66 children aged 11–13 from 16 schools and had them screen-share their real-time smartphone use over Zoom for four consecutive days. Among the 41 who played game apps, children averaged 39 minutes of game-app play across the period and were exposed to advertising for 9.7 minutes of every hour spent gaming — about 16% of game time, or 22.9 ads per hour. The single biggest ad category was other mobile games (38% of all ads), but much of the rest was adult-oriented: finance, real estate, and even alcohol. Unprompted, a third of participants said they wanted online advertising changed, and every comment about it was negative.
studies.why_it_matters: This is one of the first objective, child-captured records of in-game ad exposure rather than an estimate from parents or platforms, and it shows mobile games function as a high-frequency ad channel delivering adult categories to pre-teens.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands buying programmatic in-app inventory may have far less control over audience age than they assume — the finding is a prompt to audit where mobile placements actually land and to anticipate regulatory pressure on in-game advertising to minors.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For parents: a child's 'game time' is partly ad time, and the ads aren't just for other games — they include finance, property and alcohol. Kids themselves notice and dislike it.
studies.caveats: Small sample (66 children, 41 with game-app data) from a single region of one country; four-day observation window; children knew they were being recorded, which may have altered their behavior; descriptive rather than causal.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample, method and all reported figures (39 minutes, 9.7 min/hour, 16.2%, 22.9 ads/hour, 38.2% game ads, one-third mentioning advertising) match the abstract.

studies.title: Should your social ad show 10,000 likes or 10? It depends on whether the brand is status or substance
studies.paper_title: The effect of ad-interactor size on consumers’ purchase intention in social media in-feed ads
studies.journal: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
studies.the_study: Five experiments run on real Chinese social platforms (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, WeChat Moments) tested how the visible number of other people interacting with an in-feed ad — what the authors call 'ad-interactor size' — affects purchase intention, using both real and fictitious brands across functional and symbolic product types. For symbolic, status-signaling brands, ads showing a small interactor count produced higher purchase intention, driven by consumers' need for uniqueness. For functional brands, the reverse held: a large interactor count lifted purchase intention via need for belonging.
studies.why_it_matters: Social proof is treated as universally good in paid social, but these results suggest high visible engagement can actively undercut ads for aspirational or identity-based brands.
studies.story_angle_primary: Worth A/B testing whether surfacing or suppressing engagement counts changes conversion by brand type — a cheap creative-ops lever most teams never touch, though these are lab-style experiments on one country's platforms, not live campaign results.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A quiet explanation for why a luxury or niche brand can feel less appealing once everyone is liking it — and why popularity signals reassure us on practical purchases but deflate us on expressive ones.
studies.caveats: All studies conducted in China on Chinese platforms; experimental settings with stated purchase intention rather than observed purchases; some brands fictitious; per-condition sample sizes not reported in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Findings and mediators are reported correctly; the phrase "run on real Chinese social platforms" slightly overstates what the abstract describes and sits awkwardly with the digest's own "lab-style" caveat.

studies.title: Ad creatives are splitting into three camps on generative AI — and one is deliberately getting more human
studies.paper_title: Adapting to generative AI in creative work: a technological frames perspective on creative advertising
studies.the_study: Researchers combined three years of netnographic observation in online advertising communities with interviews with advertising creatives to map how practitioners interpret generative AI. They found competing frames around AI's creative agency, its job threat, and where value now sits in creative output. These frames drive three distinct adaptive strategies: AI skilling (learning the tools), reskilling (shifting roles), and 'deep skilling' — deliberately cultivating human capabilities that generative AI cannot easily reproduce.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives agency and in-house creative leaders a vocabulary for why AI adoption stalls or splinters inside the same team, and suggests resistance is often a coherent strategy rather than mere reluctance.
studies.story_angle_primary: Instead of a single AI mandate, consider which frame dominates each team and whether 'deep skilling' talent should be protected and priced differently from tool-fluent talent.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A look inside how the people who make the ads you see are reacting to AI — some retraining, some leaning harder into the things machines can't fake.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and interpretive, no quantitative outcomes; sample of creatives in online advertising communities, composition and size not fully specified in the abstract; findings describe perceptions and strategies, not effects on creative performance.
studies.verdict_notes: Method (three years of netnography plus interviews), the three competing frames and the skilling/reskilling/deep-skilling typology match the abstract; qualitative limits are flagged.

studies.title: How much authority an agency gives its AI depends on where the client is from
studies.paper_title: Governing AI Across Markets: How Client-Origin Expectations Shape Human-AI Collaboration in Globally Oriented Advertising Agencies in Asia
studies.the_study: Multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork across three globally oriented advertising agencies in Asia — participant observation plus semi-structured interviews with 30 practitioners — examined how AI governance works in practice. The researchers found governance is not standardized but relational: agency staff calibrate who decides, how much the AI is trusted, and who is accountable based on what they believe clients from different regions expect. A European financial services client operating under GDPR and a performance-focused Southeast Asian brand effectively get different levels of algorithmic autonomy on the same agency floor.
studies.why_it_matters: As agencies automate millions of campaign decisions daily, this shows the real constraint on AI authority is client origin and perceived regulatory culture, not the technology's capability.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brand-side marketers should ask their agencies explicitly what level of algorithmic autonomy is being applied to their account — the answer may be an assumption about their market rather than a negotiated policy.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited direct consumer angle, though it reveals that whether a human or an algorithm chose the ad you just saw can depend on the advertiser's home country.
studies.caveats: Qualitative ethnography in three agencies in Asia; all claims about client expectations are agency-side practitioner attributions, explicitly not verified with clients; findings are not statistically generalizable.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, site count and interview N are correct and the practitioner-attribution limitation is carried into Caveats; the "Why it matters" line overstates what an ethnography can show.

studies.title: When a lesson looks like an ad, parents clamp down on it
studies.paper_title: Teaching, selling or both? Exploring presumed influence effects of edu-ads on parents’ mediation intent
studies.journal: Young Consumers Insight and Ideas for Responsible Marketers
studies.the_study: An experiment with 147 parents compared reactions to three content types: a straight advertisement, an 'edu-ad' (an educational lesson packaged in persuasive ad format), and a conventional educator lesson. A serial mediation model traced how perceived amusement and informational value, perceived manipulative intent, and presumed positive impact on children fed into parents' intentions to actively discuss or restrict the content. Edu-ads occupied a distinct middle category — processed partly like entertainment, partly like commercial advertising — with consequences for how much parents would mediate children's exposure.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands and nonprofits increasingly wrap educational messaging in ad formats; this suggests the format itself can trigger parental suspicion that blunts the educational payoff.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're building branded educational content for kids, test whether the ad-like packaging that wins attention also raises perceived manipulative intent among the gatekeepers — parents — who decide whether the content survives.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For parents: a useful reminder that 'educational' content aimed at children often carries a persuasive frame, and that your instinct about whether something is teaching or selling shapes how you respond.
studies.caveats: Single experiment with N=147 across three conditions (small per-condition cells); measures stated mediation intentions rather than observed parenting behavior; stimulus-based scenario study; single-country sample.
studies.verdict_notes: Design and N are right, but the headline and "Why it matters" assert a directional result the abstract does not report; the abstract states only that the serial mediation model was supported and that edu-ads form a distinct category.

studies.title: When "diverse" virtual influencers backfire: disability avatars cut donation intent
studies.paper_title: Potential Risks of Virtual Influencer Diversity in Charitable Endorsements: A Cognitive Dissonance Perspective
studies.the_study: Two online experiments tested how diversity attributes built into computer-generated (virtual) influencers affect charitable endorsements. In Study 1 (N=256), a virtual influencer coded as an ethnic minority raised perceived attractiveness and donation intention, while one coded with a disability lowered both. Study 2 (N=623) replicated the negative effect for disability, showed it ran through cognitive dissonance in viewers, and found that a strong fit between the endorser and the cause substantially reduced that dissonance.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands and nonprofits increasingly use synthetic avatars as a low-cost, controllable way to signal inclusivity — but the research suggests that diversity attributes are not interchangeable, and that one common choice can depress the very giving the campaign is meant to drive.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're commissioning virtual influencers, treat "diversity" as a set of distinct design decisions, each needing its own pretest rather than a blanket inclusivity win; the mitigating factor here was endorser–cause fit, which is a testable lever — try pairing an avatar's represented identity with a cause it plausibly connects to and measure donation outcomes, not just sentiment.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The result is an uncomfortable mirror: audiences in these studies reacted worse to a simulated person with a disability, apparently because the synthetic-plus-disabled combination felt dissonant. It's a reminder that representation delivered by an algorithmically generated character can read very differently from representation by a real human.
studies.caveats: Online panel experiments using hypothetical charitable scenarios and stated donation intentions rather than actual giving; avatars and causes were researcher-created, so effects may hinge on specific stimulus design; cultural context of the samples is not clear from the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Both study Ns, the opposite effects for ethnicity and disability, the dissonance mechanism and the endorser–cause fit moderator are all accurate; one word overstates the fit effect.

studies.title: Watching someone else go green feels good enough — and that's the problem
studies.paper_title: Vicarious moral satisfaction: how audiences make sense of green influencers’ prosocial content and disengage from action
studies.the_study: Using focus groups, in-depth interviews and netnographic observation of social media, researchers examined how audiences actually interpret "green influencer" sustainability content. They identified a consistent three-stage pattern: viewers feel moral elevation and admiration, then experience what the authors call vicarious moral satisfaction, then shift responsibility for action onto the influencer or onto institutions. Audiences aligned themselves morally with the message while explicitly positioning themselves as behaviorally disengaged.
studies.why_it_matters: Sustainability campaigns measured on engagement — likes, admiring comments, positive sentiment — may be generating exactly the emotional response that lets audiences off the hook, with high moral approval masking zero behavior change.
studies.story_angle_primary: Question whether warm engagement metrics on purpose-driven influencer content are a leading indicator of anything; the implied test is to build content that assigns the viewer a concrete, small action rather than showcasing the influencer's virtue, and to measure downstream behavior (clicks to a product, sign-ups, repeat purchase) against admiration-only creative.
studies.story_angle_secondary: There's a tidy name now for the feeling of scrolling past someone composting, feeling genuinely inspired, and then doing nothing: vicarious moral satisfaction. Admiring other people's good behavior can function as a substitute for your own.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and interpretive — no sample sizes, control conditions or quantified effects reported in the abstract; findings describe how people talk about their responses, not measured behavior; context and country of participants unspecified, limiting generalizability.
studies.verdict_notes: Method and three-stage process reported accurately; minor overstatement in "Why it matters" ("zero behavior change") and an unverifiable detail about where responsibility is shifted.

studies.title: Sports betting ads have made gambling feel like just another part of being young
studies.paper_title: A narrative review of qualitative studies exploring the normalization of gambling for youth and younger adults
studies.the_study: Researchers synthesized 22 qualitative studies published between 2015 and 2025 on how gambling becomes normalized for people up to age 35, using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: early exposure through family and peers; pervasive gambling advertising, especially embedded in sport, that frames betting as entertaining and glamorous; smartphones and apps that push gambling into previously off-limits spaces and social situations; and young people's own calls for stricter advertising controls and counter-marketing.
studies.why_it_matters: The synthesis points to advertising — particularly sports sponsorship and broadcast integration — as a central mechanism of normalization, which is precisely the terrain regulators in several markets are moving to restrict.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone advertising in or around sport, the regulatory risk here is live: the evidence base increasingly names in-game betting promotion as a driver of youth normalization, and young people themselves are advocating for restrictions. Brands sharing sponsorship inventory with betting operators should think about adjacency and reputational spillover now rather than after the rules change.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If betting odds read like part of the match commentary to you, that's the point — the review describes how gambling got woven into sport, friendship groups and phones until it stopped registering as a distinct activity at all.
studies.caveats: This is a narrative review rather than new primary data; the underlying studies are qualitative and self-reported, cannot establish causation, and skew toward particular sociocultural settings; findings describe perceptions and social meanings, not measured gambling behavior or ad exposure.
studies.verdict_notes: Review scope, n = 22 studies, date range, age range and four themes all match; the headline asserts causation that a narrative review of qualitative studies cannot establish.

studies.title: The thing that keeps kids glued to a screen isn't the story — it's how much the picture moves
studies.paper_title: Attention Trap? How Visual Motion Shapes Children's Screen Time and Engagement on Video Platforms
studies.the_study: Researchers combined three methods to test whether raw visual motion drives children's video engagement. They analyzed more than 32,000 videos from leading children's YouTube channels and found higher optical-flow motion predicted viewership even after controlling for visual, audio and emotional features; they then produced educational videos with experimentally manipulated background motion and ran randomized YouTube ad campaigns, where higher-motion versions earned significantly higher view-rates and views; finally, a lab eye-tracking study with children showed motion works by shortening long attentional lapses — pulling kids back to the screen faster — rather than preventing look-aways, and without stealing attention from instructional content.
studies.why_it_matters: It identifies a concrete, measurable production variable — on-screen motion — that platforms, creators and advertisers can dial up or down, and that regulators could scrutinize as a design feature engineered to hold children's attention.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brands making child-directed or family content, motion intensity is a testable creative lever distinct from narrative or characters — worth A/B testing in paid campaigns, but also worth weighing against reputational risk if "attention engineering" aimed at kids becomes a regulatory flashpoint.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Parents often blame content or characters for screen fixation; this suggests a more mechanical culprit — fast-moving visuals that snap a wandering child back to the screen. It also hints that educational videos with livelier backgrounds may hold attention without hurting learning.
studies.caveats: The field experiment was run through one platform's (YouTube) advertising infrastructure, so view-rate is an ad metric rather than sustained viewing; the eye-tracking study is a lab setting and sample size is not stated in the abstract; short observation horizon and no evidence on long-term learning or wellbeing effects.
studies.verdict_notes: Three-study design, 32,000+ videos, randomized YouTube campaigns and the eye-tracking mechanism are all reported faithfully; headline and one learning claim reach slightly past the abstract.

studies.title: Tobacco ads still show up on Japanese streaming — unless you tell the platform you're 18
studies.paper_title: Tobacco advertising on TVer, Japan’s ad-supported video-on-demand platform: a commercial message content analysis
studies.the_study: Researchers manually coded every commercial break in catch-up streaming programs from four major Japanese broadcasters on the ad-supported platform TVer over five days in March 2025, measuring total commercial duration across nine ad categories. When no age was declared, tobacco advertising accounted for 1.2% of total commercial time, concentrated in variety and comedy programming. When the researchers logged in with a declared age of 18 — below Japan's legal smoking age — no tobacco ads appeared at all.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows age-gating works when triggered, but that the default anonymous viewing experience on a mainstream streaming platform still serves tobacco ads to anyone, including minors — evidence that industry self-regulation leaves a gap in digital channels.
studies.story_angle_primary: A practical warning for any advertiser relying on platform-level age gating: controls that depend on voluntary self-declared login data can be functionally absent for a large share of the audience. Brands in age-restricted categories should audit what their ads look like to a logged-out viewer.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Streaming feels like a cleaner, more controlled ad environment than broadcast TV, but the targeting safeguards consumers assume are in place often only switch on if you volunteer personal data first.
studies.caveats: Single platform, single country, and a five-day observation window; manual coding of commercial duration rather than exposure data from actual youth viewers; shows ad availability, not measured youth exposure or behavioral effect.
studies.verdict_notes: Platform, four broadcasters, 10–14 March 2025 window, nine categories, 1.2% tobacco share, variety/comedy concentration and the age-18 null result all match the abstract; caveats correctly note availability rather than measured youth exposure.

studies.title: Telling people an ad was made by AI made them trust it more, not less
studies.paper_title: Disclosure in AI-Generated Advertising: How Source Credibility Affects Consumer Purchase Intention
studies.journal: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
studies.the_study: Two experiments tested how disclosing AI involvement affects responses to advertising. Study 1 found that disclosing an ad was AI-generated increased perceived ad trustworthiness and attractiveness, which in turn improved attitudes and raised purchase intention. Study 2 compared disclosure framings and found that "behavior" disclosures — explaining what the AI did with data — raised privacy concerns, while "benefit" framings, which emphasize what consumers gain, produced more favorable ad attitudes.
studies.why_it_matters: With AI-disclosure rules tightening in several markets, this suggests compliance need not be a cost — but the wording matters, and the instinct to explain the mechanics of data use may backfire relative to explaining the payoff.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat mandated AI labels as creative copy, not legal boilerplate: test benefit-framed disclosures against procedural ones, and watch whether the apparent transparency bonus holds as AI-generated ads become the norm rather than a novelty.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The label on an ad shapes how you judge it. A brand that admits using AI may read as more honest than one that stays quiet — at least for now, while disclosure is still unusual.
studies.caveats: Two experiments with sample sizes, recruitment source and country not specified in the abstract; outcomes are stated purchase intention and attitudes, not actual purchases; likely hypothetical ad stimuli, and the trust benefit may reflect the current novelty of disclosure rather than a durable effect.
studies.verdict_notes: Both studies' directions and mechanisms match; the digest adds definitions of "behavior" and "benefit" disclosure that the abstract does not supply.

studies.title: In VR, travelers stop asking whether to trust the listing
studies.paper_title: Seeing is believing? How VR and 360-degree video bypass trust to drive approach tendencies in Airbnb advertising
studies.the_study: In a within-subject lab experiment, 306 participants viewed Airbnb listings in three formats — static images, 360-degree video, and full VR via a high-fidelity head-mounted display — and researchers modeled the paths from interactivity and vividness through mental imagery, arousal and pleasure to approach tendency. With static ads, intent was pleasure-driven and strongly conditioned on perceived trust in the transaction. In the immersive formats, responses shifted toward arousal-driven, more heuristic processing, and trust's moderating role weakened substantially.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests immersive media doesn't just make listings more appealing — it changes how consumers appraise risk, functioning as a kind of ambient verification in peer-to-peer markets where trust is normally the bottleneck.
studies.story_angle_primary: For platforms and travel brands, immersive formats may be most valuable precisely where trust is weakest: new hosts, unfamiliar destinations, unreviewed listings. But the same mechanism raises a governance question — if immersion suppresses trust scrutiny, platforms need stronger guarantees that what's shown is what's delivered.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Putting on a headset to tour a rental may make you feel you've verified it when you haven't. The sensation of "having been there" can quietly substitute for the checks — reviews, host history — you'd normally run.
studies.caveats: Controlled lab setting with a within-subject design (participants saw all three formats, which can inflate contrast effects); outcome is approach tendency, not booking or spending; single category (Airbnb listings) and a PLS-SEM path model rather than a behavioral field test; country and sample composition not specified.
studies.verdict_notes: N=306, within-subject design, three formats, HMD and PLS-SEM all correct; the headline overstates by implying trust stops mattering, when the abstract says only its moderating role is attenuated.

studies.title: Telling people your Instagram model isn't real cuts both ways
studies.paper_title: This person does not exist: Detailed AI disclosure and trust in synthetic visual brand posts
studies.the_study: In an online experiment with 606 participants, people saw a brand's Instagram post featuring a hyper-realistic human figure under one of three conditions: no disclosure, a generic "AI-generated" label, or a detailed disclosure explicitly stating that the depicted person does not exist. Trust was measured before and after participants were told the image was synthetic. Detailed disclosure had no direct effect on trust; instead it worked through two opposing channels — it reduced suspicions of manipulative intent (protecting trust) while simultaneously making the image feel more artificial (eroding trust). Younger consumers showed a stronger protective effect from the reduced manipulation inference.
studies.why_it_matters: As AI-content disclosure rules tighten across platforms and regulators, brands need to know that how specific a label is changes which psychological lever it pulls — and the two levers push trust in opposite directions.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brands running synthetic imagery should treat disclosure wording as a testable variable, not a compliance checkbox: a vague "AI-generated" tag and an explicit "this person does not exist" produce different trust dynamics, and the net effect may vary by audience age and category. Worth A/B testing disclosure language in live social campaigns before regulation dictates it.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The models in your feed may never have existed — and this research shows that being told so makes most people feel the brand is less manipulative but the image less real. It is a useful reminder to check for AI labels and to notice how much of your trust rests on a face.
studies.caveats: Online experiment with a single Instagram-style stimulus; trust was self-reported rather than measured through purchase or engagement behavior; one brand/post context; short time horizon with trust reassessed immediately after exposure.
studies.verdict_notes: N=606, the three disclosure conditions, pre/post trust measurement, the two opposing mechanisms and the age moderation of the manipulative-intent path all match the abstract.

studies.title: Dating apps beat social media for reach — but social media delivered the completions
studies.paper_title: Design and results of the promotional campaign for the “Understanding pre-exposure prophylaxis modalities for HIV prevention in European communities” (PROTECT) survey
studies.the_study: Researchers designed and ran a 2023 promotional campaign to recruit men who have sex with men, transgender and non-binary people across Europe into an online HIV prevention survey (PROTECT), using a logo, slogan, website and tailored creative placed on dating apps, social media and in print. The campaign drew 15,458 completed surveys: 55% came via dating app links and 38% via social media. Dating app ads had a click-through rate of 9.0% versus 2.1% on social media — but people who arrived from social media ads were more likely to finish the survey.
studies.why_it_matters: It is a rare real-world media comparison showing that the channel with the headline click-through rate is not necessarily the channel with the best downstream conversion — a trap in any funnel-based media plan.
studies.story_angle_primary: A concrete argument against optimizing media buys on click-through rate alone: here the high-CTR channel produced lower completion quality. Marketers should pull completion or conversion rates by source before reallocating budget, and consider dating apps as a serious, under-used paid channel for reaching specific communities.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The notion of "hard to reach" audiences often just means advertisers are buying the wrong media; when the campaign went where people already were, more than 15,000 responded.
studies.caveats: A single public-health campaign in Europe with no randomization between channels — audience self-selection, not creative or channel effects, could drive the CTR-versus-completion difference; the "product" is a survey, not a purchase, so generalization to commercial advertising is uncertain.
studies.verdict_notes: Campaign design, 15,458 completions, 55%/38% split and the 9.0% vs 2.1% CTRs are all accurate; the headline's "delivered the completions" sits oddly against dating apps supplying the majority of completed surveys.

studies.title: Major-key music needs bright color; minor-key needs muted — mismatched travel ads fall flat
studies.paper_title: The interaction effect of musical tonality and color saturation in tourism video on visit intention
studies.the_study: Two between-subjects experiments (N=308 and N=368) crossed musical tonality (major vs. minor key) with color saturation (high vs. low) in tourism promotional videos and measured intention to visit the destination. Congruent pairings won: major-key music with high saturation and minor-key music with low saturation both outperformed mismatched combinations. The two winning combinations worked through different routes — bright-and-major built a sense of "destination intimacy," while muted-and-minor drove perceived novelty — and incongruent pairings disrupted processing fluency and weakened persuasion.
studies.why_it_matters: Video ads are usually scored and color-graded by separate people at separate stages; this suggests the two decisions interact and that getting them out of sync actively costs persuasive power.
studies.story_angle_primary: A testable brief for video teams: lock soundtrack tonality and color grade as a paired decision, and pick the pair based on the emotional job — warmth and familiarity versus novelty and intrigue. Worth validating with in-platform video tests before assuming the lab effect scales.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The pull you feel toward a destination in a 30-second video may owe less to the beach than to whether the music and the color grade agree with each other.
studies.caveats: Lab-style experiments measuring stated visit intention rather than booking behavior; tourism video context only; sample details and country not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Two between-subjects experiments, N=308 and N=368, the congruent combinations, the two distinct mediators and the processing-fluency account for incongruent pairings all match the abstract.

studies.title: Labeling an ad "AI-generated" mostly produces a shrug — except among AI-savvy consumers
studies.paper_title: Ads from automatons: Consumer perceptions of AI modality disclosures and the roles of AI experience and dispositional persuasion knowledge on advertising outcomes
studies.journal: Journal of Global Scholars of Marketing Science
studies.the_study: An experiment tested consumer responses to online banner ads whose elements were disclosed as AI-generated, against a non-AI-disclosed control, while measuring participants' dispositional persuasion knowledge (their general skepticism of marketing), prior experience with AI tools, and trust in AI. Overall the researchers found general ambivalence toward AI-disclosed ads regardless of which modality was labeled. But when AI-generated text specifically was disclosed, consumers with higher dispositional persuasion knowledge, more AI experience and more trust in AI responded more positively on several advertising outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: With platform rules and proposed laws mandating AI disclosure, the fear is a blanket backlash; this suggests the average response is neutral and that the most AI-literate consumers may actually react favorably to disclosed AI copy.
studies.story_angle_primary: Disclosure may be less of a brand risk than feared — but the effect is segment-dependent, so brands should profile audience AI familiarity before deciding how prominently to label AI-assisted creative, and treat AI-written text and AI-generated imagery as separate disclosure decisions.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you use AI tools yourself, you are likely to judge an AI-made ad more generously than someone who doesn't — familiarity, not the technology, is doing the work.
studies.caveats: Single experimental study on banner ads with self-reported advertising outcomes rather than click or purchase behavior; sample size, composition and country not stated in the abstract; hypothetical ad exposure rather than real campaign conditions.
studies.verdict_notes: Banner-ad experiment, the ambivalence result and the text-disclosure moderation are reported correctly; a gloss on dispositional persuasion knowledge and a consumer angle that drops the text-only boundary need tightening.

studies.title: Eye-tracking finds moviegoers read poster colors differently than the industry assumes
studies.paper_title: Through the eyes of the viewer: colour, emotion, and genre recognition in movie marketing
studies.the_study: Two within-subjects experiments used biometric eye-tracking with 41 participants aged 18–40 to test how color palettes on movie posters map to film genres (action, animation, romantic comedy, science fiction, horror) and to emotions from Plutchik's wheel using monochrome posters. Several associations departed from industry convention — green was linked to sadness and orange to trust — and the study confirmed a strong central fixation bias, meaning placement in the poster's center heavily shaped where attention went.
studies.why_it_matters: Entertainment marketing leans on inherited color conventions for genre signaling; this is direct attention and association evidence that some of those conventions may not match how audiences actually decode a poster.
studies.story_angle_primary: Creative teams working in key art and packaging could pretest color-genre assumptions rather than inheriting them, and should remember that composition and center placement can override color in driving attention.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The poster that made you want to see a film worked on you before you read a word of it — mostly through where your eye landed first.
studies.caveats: Very small sample (N=41), narrow age range (18–40), single country context, within-subjects lab design with artificial monochrome stimuli, and no link to ticket-buying behavior.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, N (41), age range, within-subjects format, genres, Plutchik's wheel and the green/sadness and orange/trust findings all match the abstract. Issues are in framing: the digest foregrounds divergence from convention while the abstract reports both alignment and divergence, a story angle claims placement can 'override' color (not a comparison the abstract makes), and the 'single country context' caveat is not supported by the abstract.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **AI authorship is not the thing consumers punish.** The previous digest established this through backlash analysis and qualitative work — "Coke's AI Christmas ad drew 7,800 comments" (W7204147563), "Older consumers don't reject AI-made ads" (W7214074450), "Consumers preferred AI-made ads to human-made ones" (W7203605245). The new batch converges from the experimental side: "Telling people an ad was made by AI made them trust it more, not less" (W7207577485) and "Labeling an ad 'AI-generated' mostly produces a shrug" (W7211870608) both find neutral-to-positive responses to disclosure. The accumulating evidence now points the same way across methods, samples and countries.
- **Processing fluency and congruence keep showing up as the mechanism.** "Major-key music needs bright color" (W7213228572) joins last run's "When a clever visual metaphor confuses people" (W7204599802) and "Cute mascots should talk about warmth" (W7204255947): mismatched creative elements disrupt fluency and cost persuasion, regardless of which elements are mismatched.
- **Headline metrics keep failing as proxies for outcomes.** "Dating apps beat social media for reach — but social media delivered the completions" (W7214195424) extends the previous run's "Eight brands switched off their branded search ads" (W7204491303) and "Text-heavy social ads get remembered — just not the brand" (W7212195252). Clicks, recall and reach each decouple from the thing the advertiser actually wants.
- **Where the ad budget goes under pressure.** "Slashing the ad budget makes your stock look riskier" (W7214298879) pairs directly with "When family firms miss their targets, they cut ads and spend on CSR instead" (W7212229180): one study shows who cuts first, the other prices what the cut costs in the equity market.
- **Virtual endorsers work only under conditions.** "When 'diverse' virtual influencers backfire" (W7202162669) reinforces "Pairing a virtual influencer with a human one works — but only if the ad keeps its distance" (W7213402036). Both find synthetic endorsers are a set of separate design bets, not a uniform modernization.

**Advances**

- **From practitioner unease to organizational structure.** Last run captured tourism marketers improvising ethics around deepfake imagery (W7213453650). This run moves to how firms actually organize around AI: "Ad creatives are splitting into three camps on generative AI" (W7204571530) names skilling, reskilling and "deep skilling" as competing strategies, and "How much authority an agency gives its AI depends on where the client is from" (W7213885424) shows governance is calibrated to perceived client regulatory culture rather than set by policy.
- **Disclosure research gets granular.** Having established that labels don't automatically hurt, the field has moved to wording and modality: benefit versus behavior framing (W7207577485), generic "AI-generated" tags versus "this person does not exist" (W7212138832), and AI-generated text versus imagery as separate disclosure decisions (W7211870608).
- **Green communications moves from message components to messenger.** "Guilt-based green ads only work when all three ingredients are present" (W7172220713) specified what has to be in the message; "Let the AI do the guilt-tripping" (W7216305737) now shows the same appeal lands differently depending on whether a human or a machine signs it — with a field-experiment leg using real purchase data.

**Counterpoints**

- **Detection is not disclosure.** "When shoppers spot an AI-made ad, they like it less — but still buy" (W7214625312) cuts against the broadly reassuring disclosure literature above: being told costs nothing, being caught costs brand attitude. That distinction was not visible in last run's set.
- **Social proof is conditional, not weak.** "What actually makes mobile ads work" (W7204247420) found subjective norms barely registered. "Should your social ad show 10,000 likes or 10?" (W7220966006) suggests the reason may be aggregation: visible engagement lifts functional brands and depresses symbolic ones, so averaged across categories the effect looks close to zero.
- **Engagement on purpose-driven content may be an anti-indicator.** "Watching someone else go green feels good enough" (W7203716020) complicates the previous run's green-claims meta-analysis (W7202096496) by arguing admiration and positive sentiment can substitute for action rather than predict it.

**New themes**

- **Children and young people as a measured, not estimated, advertising audience** — effectively absent last run beyond the #womenshealth content analysis (W7214105022). Now five studies: in-game ad exposure captured by children themselves (W7214801403), motion as an engineered attention lever in kids' video (W7214311385), default-setting tobacco ads on Japanese streaming (W7203907887), gambling normalization among under-35s (W7207692856) and parental gatekeeping of edu-ads (W7116214838).
- **Immersive media changing how risk is appraised** — "In VR, travelers stop asking whether to trust the listing" (W7204201453) is a genuinely new line with no prior-run analogue.
- **Capital-markets consequences of marketing decisions** — W7214298879 is the first finance-side advertising study across these two runs.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch mark a shift from estimating children's advertising exposure to measuring it directly — and the measurements are unflattering. Children screen-sharing their own phones logged 22.9 ads per hour of mobile gaming, including finance, real estate and alcohol ("Kids recorded their own screens for four days," W7214801403); tobacco ads ran in 1.2% of commercial time on a mainstream Japanese streaming platform but vanished the moment an age was declared ("Tobacco ads still show up on Japanese streaming," W7203907887); randomized YouTube ad campaigns showed raw visual motion mechanically pulls children's attention back to the screen ("The thing that keeps kids glued to a screen," W7214311385); a synthesis of 22 studies traced youth gambling normalization substantially to sports advertising (W7207692856); and parents reacted to ad-formatted educational content with measurable suspicion ("When a lesson looks like an ad," W7116214838). Together they describe an environment where safeguards are opt-in, exposure is high-frequency, and the design variables that hold children's attention are now quantified.

**Why pitch this now:** Children's online-safety codes, gambling-advertising restrictions and scrutiny of in-game and in-app ad inventory are all moving through regulators in the UK, EU and Australia at once — and brands buying programmatic mobile inventory are, on this evidence, far less sure than they assume about who is seeing their ads.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the collapse of the gap between what the ad industry assumes about age-gating and what researchers can now measure — written for media buyers and brand-safety leads, with a parallel track for parents who have never seen the per-hour numbers. The strongest reporting hook is methodological: children, not platforms, produced the exposure data.

**Potential headlines:**
- Children recorded their own phones for four days. The ads were for alcohol, finance and real estate.
- The age check works perfectly. Almost nobody triggers it.
- Your child's game time is ad time — and nobody is counting it but researchers

**Potential outlets:**
- **Digiday** — the programmatic in-app and age-signal failure is squarely their beat, and the buy-side implication (you don't know the age of your audience) is a story their readers can act on.
- **Wired** — the optical-flow motion finding gives them a design-and-attention-engineering story with randomized field evidence behind it, not just anecdote.
- **The Guardian** — has sustained coverage of gambling advertising and children's screen exposure, and would run the parent-facing exposure numbers alongside the regulatory thread.
- **Ad Age** — well positioned for the industry-accountability framing: self-regulation in age-restricted categories measured and found wanting on a mainstream platform.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **When shoppers spot an AI-made ad, they like it less — but still buy (Work ID W7214625312):** The split between brand sentiment and purchase intent gives brands a way to price the risk of synthetic stunt creative — worth separating the two metrics instead of assuming one tracks the other, for a creative-effectiveness column or a marketing-trade news brief.
- **Slashing the ad budget makes your stock look riskier (Work ID W7214298879):** A finance-department argument against cliff-edge marketing cuts, built on 231,000 firm-years — for a CFO-facing business column or a CMO/CFO-relationship feature.
- **Let the AI do the guilt-tripping and keep the humans for the pep talk (Work ID W7216305737):** Disclosed AI authorship defuses the resentment a human scold provokes, so sustainability teams should match authorship to appeal type — for a sustainability-communications or cause-marketing column.
- **Abstract nature imagery outperforms actual forests in service ads (Work ID W7220455699):** The stock-photo waterfall may be the weaker choice; novelty and mystery, not calm, do the persuasive work — for a creative-strategy trade column or a design/branding explainer.
- **Kids recorded their own screens for four days (Work ID W7214801403):** The headline exposure numbers plus the adult ad categories make this a strong standalone for a general-interest parenting or technology section, with a buy-side version for an adtech trade on in-app audience uncertainty.
- **Should your social ad show 10,000 likes or 10? (Work ID W7220966006):** Social proof can backfire for aspirational brands — a cheap, untested creative-ops lever, for a paid-social trade explainer or a luxury-marketing column.
- **Ad creatives are splitting into three camps on generative AI (Work ID W7204571530):** "Deep skilling" as a deliberate strategy reframes AI resistance as a talent-pricing question rather than reluctance — for an agency-trade feature or a creative-leadership column.
- **How much authority an agency gives its AI depends on where the client is from (Work ID W7213885424):** Brand-side marketers almost certainly don't know what level of algorithmic autonomy their account is getting — for an agency/client-relationship trade piece or a marketing-procurement column.
- **When a lesson looks like an ad, parents clamp down on it (Work ID W7116214838):** The packaging that wins children's attention raises parents' suspicion, which decides whether the content survives at all — for a kids-media or branded-content trade explainer.
- **When "diverse" virtual influencers backfire (Work ID W7202162669):** Diversity attributes in synthetic avatars are not interchangeable, and endorser–cause fit is the mitigating lever — for a nonprofit/fundraising trade piece, with a careful consumer-psychology treatment in a general-interest outlet.
- **Watching someone else go green feels good enough (Work ID W7203716020):** "Vicarious moral satisfaction" gives a name to the problem with engagement-measured purpose campaigns — for a CMO-audience column on purpose marketing, and a consumer-psychology explainer for general readers.
- **Sports betting ads have made gambling feel like just another part of being young (Work ID W7207692856):** Reputational and regulatory adjacency risk for non-betting brands sharing sports sponsorship inventory — for a sports-marketing or sponsorship trade feature.
- **The thing that keeps kids glued to a screen isn't the story (Work ID W7214311385):** Randomized evidence that on-screen motion is a dial creators and advertisers can turn, with a regulatory shadow over "attention engineering" — for a technology or science section in a general-interest outlet.
- **Tobacco ads still show up on Japanese streaming (Work ID W7203907887):** Age-gating that only activates when a viewer volunteers data is a brand-safety gap any age-restricted advertiser should audit — for an adtech or brand-safety trade news story.
- **Telling people an ad was made by AI made them trust it more, not less (Work ID W7207577485):** Benefit-framed disclosures beat procedural ones, so mandated AI labels should be written by copywriters, not lawyers — for a marketing-trade news brief or a compliance-meets-creative column.
- **In VR, travelers stop asking whether to trust the listing (Work ID W7204201453):** Immersion appears to suppress trust scrutiny, which is commercially useful and ethically awkward for peer-to-peer platforms — for a travel-trade feature or a consumer-protection angle in a personal-finance section.
- **Telling people your Instagram model isn't real cuts both ways (Work ID W7212138832):** A detailed "this person does not exist" label and a generic AI tag pull opposite psychological levers — for a social-media marketing trade brief with an A/B test prescription.
- **Dating apps beat social media for reach — but social media delivered the completions (Work ID W7214195424):** A clean case against optimizing on click-through rate, plus an argument for dating apps as under-used paid inventory — for a media-planning trade explainer or a health-marketing piece.
- **Major-key music needs bright color; minor-key needs muted (Work ID W7213228572):** Soundtrack and color grade are normally decided by different people at different stages; this says the decisions interact — for a video-production or creative-effectiveness column.
- **Labeling an ad "AI-generated" mostly produces a shrug (Work ID W7211870608):** The AI-literate are the most forgiving audience for disclosed AI copy, which inverts the usual segmentation instinct — for a marketing-trade news brief.
- **Eye-tracking finds moviegoers read poster colors differently than the industry assumes (Work ID W7213276828):** Inherited color-genre conventions may not match how audiences decode key art, and center placement outweighs color for attention — for an entertainment-marketing trade piece (flag the N=41 sample).

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Advertising — 2026-10-09
**Checked:** 2026-10-09 | **Studies reviewed:** 21
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: When shoppers spot an AI-made ad, they like it less — but still buy
**Work ID:** W7214625312 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Intention stated as behavior in headline** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "When shoppers spot an AI-made ad, they like it less — but still buy"
- **Abstract says:** "Consumers who realize an advertisement is synthetic experience diminished positive attitudes toward the advertisement and the brand, but it does not impact purchase intent or social media engagement."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports no effect on self-reported purchase intent, not on purchases. "Still buy" tells readers behavior was measured and unchanged, which the study does not show (the digest's own caveat acknowledges self-report).
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to something like "...they like it less — but say they'd still buy" or "...but purchase intent holds steady"."

**Issue B. Direction of moderation not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "high creativity softened the attitude penalty"
- **Abstract says:** "Lastly, creativity moderates the relationship between awareness of an advertisement's falsity and attitudes towards the advertisement and the brand."
- **Problem:** The abstract states only that creativity moderates the relationship; it does not say in which direction. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "creativity moderated the link between noticing the ad was fake and attitudes" without specifying the direction, or verify the direction in the full text."

### Study 2: Slashing the ad budget makes your stock look riskier, 231,000 firm-years suggest
**Work ID:** W7214298879 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Let the AI do the guilt-tripping and keep the humans for the pep talk
**Work ID:** W7216305737 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Dropped moderator (attribution focus)** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "AI-generated guilt appeals beat human-generated ones at driving green purchase intention, apparently because an AI scold triggers less "green moral pressure." Human-generated encouragement beat AI-generated encouragement, working through greater green self-efficacy."
- **Abstract says:** "Furthermore, attribution focus moderates these interaction effects: behavioral attribution strengthens the advantage of AI-generated guilt appeal, whereas personal attribution strengthens the advantage of human-generated encouragement appeal."
- **Problem:** The digest presents the creator-type × appeal effects as unconditional and omits the named boundary condition, so readers may assume the pairing rule holds regardless of how the message frames attribution.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add a sentence noting that the advantages were strengthened by behavioral attribution (for AI guilt) and personal attribution (for human encouragement)."

### Study 4: Abstract nature imagery outperforms actual forests in service ads
**Work ID:** W7220455699 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: Kids recorded their own screens for four days — and found an ad every 2.6 minutes of gaming
**Work ID:** W7214801403 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: Should your social ad show 10,000 likes or 10? It depends on whether the brand is status or substance
**Work ID:** W7220966006 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Setting described as live platforms** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Five experiments run on real Chinese social platforms (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, WeChat Moments)"
- **Abstract says:** "Five experimental studies using different social media (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, and WeChat Moments) and different types of products from real or virtual brands are conducted"
- **Problem:** The abstract says the experiments used these platforms as stimulus contexts, not that they were fielded as live campaigns on them; the digest's own caveat and story angle say these are not live campaign results, so the body text reads as inconsistent.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "Five experiments using in-feed ad stimuli from Chinese platforms (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, WeChat Moments)"."

### Study 7: Ad creatives are splitting into three camps on generative AI — and one is deliberately getting more human
**Work ID:** W7204571530 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 8: How much authority an agency gives its AI depends on where the client is from
**Work ID:** W7213885424 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Overstated causal/exclusive claim in Why it matters** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this shows the real constraint on AI authority is client origin and perceived regulatory culture, not the technology's capability"
- **Abstract says:** "this paper develops evidence that AI governance is not standardized but relational: it is shaped by client-origin governance expectations as attributed by agency-side practitioners... introduce client-origin governance expectations as the moderating construct explaining this variation across clients, one that capability-based and institutional accounts alone cannot address"
- **Problem:** The abstract positions client-origin expectations as a moderating construct that capability-based accounts alone cannot explain, not as a replacement for capability; "shows the real constraint" is stronger than an interpretive three-agency ethnography supports.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "suggests that client-origin expectations, not just the technology's capability, shape how much authority AI is given"."

### Study 9: When a lesson looks like an ad, parents clamp down on it
**Work ID:** W7116214838 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts unreported direction** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "When a lesson looks like an ad, parents clamp down on it"
- **Abstract says:** "The serial mediation model proposed is statistically supported, offering a possible explanation for how parents are differentially psychologically processing the three forms of media... Findings highlight that edu-ads are a distinct category of media"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports no comparative direction showing that edu-ads increase restrictive mediation relative to the other formats. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe to the reported result, e.g. "Parents process 'edu-ads' differently from both ads and lessons — and that shapes how they mediate"."

**Issue B. Why it matters goes beyond reported findings** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "this suggests the format itself can trigger parental suspicion that blunts the educational payoff"
- **Abstract says:** "Mediators include perceived amusement value, perceived informational value, perceived manipulative intent, presumed positive impact and active mediation intent... The serial mediation model proposed is statistically supported"
- **Problem:** Perceived manipulative intent is listed as a mediator, but the abstract does not report that edu-ads raised it or that any educational payoff was reduced.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the study maps how perceptions of manipulative intent and presumed impact feed into mediation decisions, without claiming edu-ads trigger suspicion or blunt learning."

**Issue C. Outcome variable described loosely** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "fed into parents' intentions to actively discuss or restrict the content"
- **Abstract says:** "this experiment (N = 147) tests a serial mediation model exploring the effects of advertisements, edu-ads and educator lessons on parents' restrictive mediation intent. Mediators include... active mediation intent."
- **Problem:** Active mediation intent is a mediator in the model; the dependent variable is restrictive mediation intent. The digest presents both as the outcome.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that restrictive mediation intent was the outcome, with active mediation intent one of the mediators."

### Study 10: When "diverse" virtual influencers backfire: disability avatars cut donation intent
**Work ID:** W7202162669 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Substantially" overstates "significantly"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "found that a strong fit between the endorser and the cause substantially reduced that dissonance"
- **Abstract says:** "demonstrates that higher endorser–cause fit significantly reduces audiences' cognitive dissonance"
- **Problem:** "Significantly" here denotes statistical significance; "substantially" implies a large effect size the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "significantly reduced" or "reduced"."

### Study 11: Watching someone else go green feels good enough — and that's the problem
**Work ID:** W7203716020 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Zero behavior change" overstates a qualitative finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "may be generating exactly the emotional response that lets audiences off the hook, with high moral approval masking zero behavior change."
- **Abstract says:** "In practical terms, we show how moral engagement with prosocial communication may not translate into behavioral participation."
- **Problem:** The study is interpretive and measured no behavior, so it cannot show that behavior change is "zero" — only that participants positioned themselves as behaviorally disengaged. The digest's own caveat says behavior was not measured, which this line sits awkwardly against.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "with high moral approval potentially coexisting with little or no behavioural participation, as participants described themselves.""

**Issue B. Targets of responsibility shifting not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "then shift responsibility for action onto the influencer or onto institutions"
- **Abstract says:** "We identify a three-stage process in which moral elevation, vicarious moral satisfaction, and responsibility shifting shape audience responses to prosocial influencer content."
- **Problem:** The abstract names "responsibility shifting" but does not specify that responsibility is shifted onto influencers or institutions. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Either drop the specific targets or mark them as detail drawn from the full paper."

### Study 12: Sports betting ads have made gambling feel like just another part of being young
**Work ID:** W7207692856 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal headline for a qualitative narrative review** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Sports betting ads have made gambling feel like just another part of being young"
- **Abstract says:** "Second, exposure to gambling advertising, particularly through sport, was a pervasive driver of normalization, framing gambling as entertaining, glamorous, and overwhelmingly positive."
- **Problem:** The headline states advertising caused normalization, while the evidence is a thematic synthesis of qualitative, self-reported accounts — the digest's own caveat notes causation cannot be established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "Young people describe sports betting ads as making gambling feel like just another part of being young.""

### Study 13: The thing that keeps kids glued to a screen isn't the story — it's how much the picture moves
**Work ID:** W7214311385 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline rules out narrative, which was not tested** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The thing that keeps kids glued to a screen isn't the story — it's how much the picture moves"
- **Abstract says:** "higher visual motion significantly predicts video viewership after accounting for a broad set of visual, audio, and affective characteristics"
- **Problem:** The studies controlled for visual, audio and affective features and manipulated motion; they did not test narrative or story quality against motion, so the exclusive "isn't the story" framing goes beyond the evidence.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as "One measurable driver of children's viewing isn't content quality at all — it's how much the picture moves.""

**Issue B. Learning outcomes not measured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It also hints that educational videos with livelier backgrounds may hold attention without hurting learning."
- **Abstract says:** "motion increases attention to background regions without reducing attention to instructional content"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports attention to instructional content, not comprehension or learning outcomes; "without hurting learning" substitutes an untested outcome for a measured attention metric.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "may hold attention without pulling attention away from the instructional content itself (learning was not measured).""

### Study 14: Tobacco ads still show up on Japanese streaming — unless you tell the platform you're 18
**Work ID:** W7203907887 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 15: Telling people an ad was made by AI made them trust it more, not less
**Work ID:** W7207577485 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Definitions of disclosure types not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** ""behavior" disclosures — explaining what the AI did with data — raised privacy concerns, while "benefit" framings, which emphasize what consumers gain, produced more favorable ad attitudes"
- **Abstract says:** "The result reveals that behavior disclosure raises perceived privacy concerns, whereas benefit disclosure enhances attitudes toward ads among various disclosure types."
- **Problem:** The abstract names the two framings but never defines them; the digest's glosses ("what the AI did with data", "what consumers gain") are interpretation. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop the parenthetical definitions or attribute them explicitly to the full paper."

### Study 16: In VR, travelers stop asking whether to trust the listing

### Study 20: Labeling an ad "AI-generated" mostly produces a shrug — except among AI-savvy consumers
**Work ID:** W7211870608 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Dispositional persuasion knowledge glossed as "skepticism"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "dispositional persuasion knowledge (their general skepticism of marketing)"
- **Abstract says:** "the interaction of dispositional persuasion knowledge, experience with AI tools, and trust in AI"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not define dispositional persuasion knowledge; it is generally understood as a standing understanding of persuasion tactics rather than skepticism per se. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Describe it as "their general awareness of how marketing tries to persuade" or drop the parenthetical."

**Issue B. Consumer angle drops the AI-text boundary condition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "If you use AI tools yourself, you are likely to judge an AI-made ad more generously than someone who doesn't"
- **Abstract says:** "novel positive effects of dispositional persuasion knowledge, AI experience, and trust in AI with regard to specific advertising-focused dependent variables when the use of AI-generated text in ads is disclosed"
- **Problem:** The favourable response applied specifically when AI-generated text was disclosed, and only on certain outcomes; the consumer-facing line generalizes it to any AI-made ad.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add the qualifier: "...more generously when it's the ad copy that's labelled as AI-written.""

### Study 21: Eye-tracking finds moviegoers read poster colors differently than the industry assumes
**Work ID:** W7213276828 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Placement vs. color comparison not in abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "should remember that composition and center placement can override color in driving attention"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings also confirm central fixation bias, underscoring the influence of spatial placement on visual attention."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a central fixation bias but never tests or claims that spatial placement outweighs or 'overrides' colour in driving attention. The digest turns a descriptive finding into a relative ranking of two creative variables, which a creative team could act on incorrectly.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rewrite as: 'and should remember that where an element sits on the poster shapes attention in its own right — the study confirms a central fixation bias.'"

**Issue B. One-sided summary of colour-convention results** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Several associations departed from industry convention"
- **Abstract says:** "Results reveal both alignment and divergence from traditional colour-genre conventions, such as the unexpected association of green with sadness and orange with trust"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports alignment as well as divergence; the headline and study summary present only the divergence, slightly overstating how far audience perceptions depart from convention.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add that results showed both alignment and divergence, e.g. 'Some associations matched industry convention while several departed from it — green was linked to sadness and orange to trust.'"

**Issue C. Unsupported country caveat** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "single country context"
- **Abstract says:** "two experimental within-subjects studies were conducted with 41 participants aged 18 to 40"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state the participants' country or whether the sample was drawn from one country. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'country and recruitment source not specified in the abstract'."

**Issue D. Overstated intensifier on fixation bias** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the study confirmed a strong central fixation bias, meaning placement in the poster's center heavily shaped where attention went"
- **Abstract says:** "Findings also confirm central fixation bias, underscoring the influence of spatial placement on visual attention."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives no effect size or magnitude; 'strong' and 'heavily' add emphasis the abstract does not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop 'strong' and 'heavily': 'the study confirmed a central fixation bias, indicating that spatial placement influenced where attention went.'"

**Issue E. Consumer angle overstates mechanism** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The poster that made you want to see a film worked on you before you read a word of it — mostly through where your eye landed first."
- **Abstract says:** "Results reveal both alignment and divergence from traditional colour-genre conventions... Findings also confirm central fixation bias, underscoring the influence of spatial placement on visual attention."
- **Problem:** The study measured attention and colour–genre/emotion associations, not intention to see a film, and it does not establish that gaze placement is the dominant driver ('mostly').
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as: 'Where your eye lands on a poster, and the colours used, shape your first impression of a film before you read a word — though the study measured attention and associations, not ticket buying.'"
